points.description: Translates to a tree: the triangles are vertices of the dual graph, two joined when they share a diagonal. This is a tree with 18n vertices and 18n-1 edges (the diagonals) and maximum degree 3. Removing one diagonal gives two parts, and removing two gives three parts. The sizes of the parts count triangles.

levels.says: Dual tree is mentioned but its degree bound or the cut-to-parts correspondence is not stated or used.

points.description: Finds a first balanced vertex or diagonal. For example, a centroid triangle v such that each component of the tree minus v has at most 9n triangles. Equivalent: a diagonal with one side of at least 3n triangles chosen so that the argument can continue. Existence must be justified, for example by walking toward the larger component.

levels.says: Chooses such a vertex or diagonal but gives no justification that it exists.

points.description: Case where all components at v are at least 3n (three components a, b, c with sizes in [3n, 9n]). Cuts two of the three diagonals at v. The parts are a, b and c+1, and c+1 < 9n because c is the smallest component (c ≤ (18n-1)/3). All three parts are shown to lie in [3n, 9n].

levels.says: Chooses the cuts correctly but does not verify the upper bound on the third part.

points.description: Case where the smallest component is under 3n (or v has degree at most 2). Then the two largest components satisfy a ≥ b ≥ 6n-1 (a ≥ 7n). Cuts the diagonal to the component a, which has size at most 9n. Then finds a second diagonal inside the b-component by taking the deepest subtree of size at least 3n. Its size x satisfies 3n ≤ x ≤ 6n-1 since each vertex has at most 2 children. The middle part 18n-a-x is verified to lie in [3n, 9n]. Any valid different case analysis with all three bounds checked earns full marks.

levels.says: Sets up the first cut and the idea of cutting inside the larger remaining side, but the second cut is not located or its size is not bounded.
Complete construction, but one of the three size bounds is unchecked or slightly wrong.

rubric.notes: Full marks need a valid choice of two diagonals with all three part sizes checked to lie in [3n, 9n]. Part marks go for the dual tree, the first balanced cut and a partly worked case analysis. An argument that cuts once and then re-applies the argument on one side without keeping the same hypotheses should lose the P4 marks. A bare assertion that the cuts exist earns nothing beyond P1.
rubric.answer_key:
Dual tree T: 18n vertices (triangles), max degree 3, edges = diagonals. Take a centroid v: every component of T−v has ≤ 9n vertices. The component sizes a ≥ b ≥ c sum to 18n−1 (c = 0 if v has degree < 3).
Case 1, c ≥ 3n: cut the edges from v to the a- and b-components. The parts have sizes a, b, c+1. All are in [3n, 9n], since c+1 ≤ (18n−1)/3 + 1 < 9n.
Case 2, c < 3n: then a+b > 15n−1 and a ≤ 9n, so b ≥ 6n−1 and a ≥ 7n. Cut the edge from v to the a-component, giving a part of size a ∈ [7n, 9n]. In the b-component, with root w adjacent to v, take a vertex u of minimal depth-below such that its subtree has size x ≥ 3n. Its children subtrees are each < 3n and u has ≤ 2 children, so 3n ≤ x ≤ 6n−1. Cut the edge from u to its parent (or the edge vw if u = w). The middle part has size 18n−a−x ≥ 18n−9n−(6n−1) = 3n+1, and ≤ 18n−7n−3n = 8n ≤ 9n. All three parts lie in [3n, 9n]. ∎
